newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Patten urges against dictatorial tendencies.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten urges against dictatorial tendencies.

text.p: Hong Kong's outgoing Governor Chris Patten on Monday urged his successor Tung Chee-hwa not to be autocratic and said Britain was handing over the colony to China in superb economic shape.
Patten, echoing a call made by the Group of Seven at their Denver summit on maintaining Hong Kong's freedoms under Beijing's rule, said Tung should listen to people's advice.

"In Hong Kong, there is no one who has absolute power," Britain's 28th and last governor told the Chinese-language paper Ming Pao in an interview marking the end of 156 years of colonial rule in seven days' time.
Patten, alluding to his democratic reforms which have been vilified by Beijing, also told Radio Hong Kong in another interview : "I don't think... you can turn the clock back."

In their summit communique, the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- together with Russia called on China to maintain its commitments to respect Hong Kong's freedoms.
The capitalist colony, one of the world's most buoyant economies, is being handed back to communist China under a "one country, two systems" formula that guarantees it autonomy for the next 50 years.

Former shipping magnate Tung extended an olive branch to democrat activists who have mocked him as a puppet of Beijing and promised to stage handover protests when the eyes of the world media will be focused on Hong Kong.
"I hope those in the democratic camp will move on with us," Tung told the South China Morning Post.
"I assure Hong Kong people that they will be able to continue with their free lifestyle and that lawful and peaceful demonstrations will definitely be allowed in future in Hong Kong," he said.
But he made clear at a weekend news conference that new laws restricting demonstrations would take effect from the minute the territory becomes part of China on the stroke of midnight on June 30.

A public opinion poll in the Post on Monday said almost 80 percent of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people were confident about the economic future under Chinese rule, but only one in two were confident about political freedom.
The stock market, fuelled by "red chip" euphoria, soared to record levels last Friday and analysts said it could shoot up even higher in the last week of British rule.
Hong Kong's economy is poised for 5.5 percent growth this year.
The Royal Yacht Britannia sailed into Hong Kong harbour on a grey and wet Monday morning, marking the beginning of the end for Britain's Asian empire.
Patten sails away after the midnight handover ceremony on the Britannia with heir-to-the throne Prince Charles.
He said Britain could be proud to be handing over a buoyant Hong Kong blessed with civil liberties.

"The real economy is in very good health. We are growing now rather faster again, investment levels are very good, our public finances are in superb shape. That is the real economy and it couldn't be much better," he said.
Asked if he feared Hong Kong's reserves might be used to fund Chinese mainland developments, he said: "I know what I think the people of Hong Kong would expect.

"This money is the fruit of their work and endeavours over the years and it should be invested for the best interests of Hong Kong. I think a lot of people would need some persuading that spending it outside Hong Kong was in their best interests."
